Systematic ablations show that minimal demographic descriptions achieve lower mean error than richer persona configurations, while relative qualitative cues substantially outperform the tested quantitative anchors. We additionally compare these configurations with direct-prior and rule-based baselines and with alternative LLM configurations.

items.title: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuned (FT) derivatives of large language models (LLMs) are now released in large numbers, yet their provenance relies on self-reports and cannot be verified. Misattributed lineage leaves a verifier unable to audit outsourced fine-tuning, confirm license compliance of derived models, or trace vulnerabilities that a parent passes to its children. All three require the direction of derivation, not merely its presence. Existing output-only methods are limited to pairwise derivation tests or undirected lineage estimation, while recovering a directed tree requires white-box access to model weights. We formalize the problem of reconstructing a directed model tree, including internal nodes, under gray-box access, where only teacher-forced log-likelihoods are observed and weights are never inspected. Fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of the training data, and a child inherits this increase from its parent. Building on this property, we define an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between any two models as a trace of fine-tuning history, and derive from it an edge weight for each ordered pair of models. We propose TRACE-Edge, which exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree under these edge weights, with neither hyperparameters nor tree-structure constraints. We evaluate it on five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks. TRACE-Edge achieves a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 when probed with the fine-tuning examples, and on average outperforms an output-similarity baseline even with held-out probes drawn from the same distribution as the training data.

items.title: Learning to Restart: Differentiable Restart Policies for Optimization Dynamics
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive restart mechanisms, which reset the momentum or other auxiliary state of an iterative optimizer, play a central role in the empirical performance of accelerated first-order methods, yet existing restart rules remain almost entirely hand-designed. The obstruction to learning restart policies is that, unlike the typical Learning to Optimize (L2O) setting, the discrete restart events make the resulting trajectory non-differentiable in the algorithm parameters and thus block gradient-based optimization of the restart policy. We resolve this obstruction by developing a differentiable framework for restart policies through their continuous-time limit. We introduce surrogate gradients for the restart events and optimization trajectories that are efficient to compute and provably converge to their continuous-time counterparts. We validate the effectiveness of our surrogate gradients in L2O settings, training restart policies that improve upon standard handcrafted adaptive restart criteria on quadratic and linear programs, and that transfer zero-shot from synthetic quadratics to logistic regression on real datasets.

items.title: SSF-Net: A Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network for Accurate PDE Operator Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) significantly improve computational efficiency over traditional numerical solvers such as finite element method (FEM). However, PDE dynamics inherently span both local and global dynamics: disturbances propagate and decay gradually through the domain, while global coupling effects can influence the whole system simultaneously. Capturing both types of dynamics with a low complexity model remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose the Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network (SSF-Net), built around a dual-branch Spatial-Spectral Fusion (SSF) block comprising a spatial branch and a spectral branch. The spatial branch employs a multi-directional Mamba, which mitigates its inherent causal, single-direction scanning bias and capture local interactions with reduced directional bias at linear complexity. The spectral branch leverages a Fourier transform with a block-diagonal MLP to efficiently capture global spectral features with reduced parameter count and complexity. The SSF block is embedded in a multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder, which extracts multi-scale features. We evaluate SSF-Net on a comprehensive PDE benchmark spanning multiple task types and assess its long-horizon stability. Compared with attention-based and convolution-based baselines, SSF-Net achieves lower prediction error with fewer parameters while retaining near-linear asymptotic complexity in the number of spatial tokens.

items.title: Composable Causality: A Toolkit for Systematic Time-Series Causal Discovery and Treatment-Effect Benchmarking
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world multivariate time series rarely come with verified ground-truth causal structure, so research on time-series causal discovery and treatment-effect estimation depends on synthetic data. Existing tools are either fixed datasets that cannot be modified after release or script-based generators in which each script fixes one combination of mechanism, confounding, and missingness. Neither supports controlled experiments that vary a single property, such as sparsity, noise distribution, or missingness mechanism, while holding the others fixed. Counterfactual evaluation has the same gap, since existing simulators are built per paper with hardcoded mechanisms or produce observational data only. We introduce DTCD (Datasets and Toolkit for Causal Discovery), a data generation library that produces multivariate time series with ground-truth contemporaneous and lagged adjacency matrices. Topology, mechanism, noise, observational mask, and intervention policy are independent components that compose through configuration alone. Paired counterfactual twins, produced by caching the stochastic realization during the factual rollout and re-injecting it during the interventional rollout, recover individual treatment effects to numerical precision. A reference benchmark of eight discovery algorithms on eighty-one configurations and four treatment-effect estimators on eighteen configurations exposes failure modes that aggregate metrics hide. These include the inability of standard discovery methods to handle missing values, regardless of whether the missingness mechanism is informative, and a marginal-variance shortcut (varsortability) that we measure and remove by standardization. Code and data: https://github.com/hferdous/Composable_Causality

items.title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.

items.title: Ordered Policy Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.

items.title: Surrogate Quality Score: A Novel Composite Performance Metric for Model Selection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing reliance on high-fidelity, state-of-the-art machine learning based models for engineering decision-making necessitates robust and systematic approaches for model selection. While high predictive accuracy at untrained points is a necessary trait in the final model, other attributes such as model complexity, forecastability, explainability, scalability, and physics-awareness may be equally important or relevant criteria depending on application context and user requirements. In this work, we propose a novel composite performance metric, Surrogate Quality Score (SQS) for model selection based on predictive accuracy and model complexity simultaneously. SQS heuristically integrates these two attributes through a weighted product of normalized measures, yielding a unified score to reflect overall model quality. A user-specified parameter in SQS enables explicit control over the accuracy-complexity trade-off, thereby incorporating human judgement and preference in the model selection process. We extensively discuss and justify the formulation of SQS and demonstrate its utility through an illustrative example. By combining predictive accuracy and model complexity, SQS offers a systematic and objective approach for model selection based on both attributes.

items.title: Accuracy Is Not Value: Choosing Weak Supervisors by What the Student Inherits
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Weak supervisors are usually judged by their own errors, but what matters is what a student learns from them. For squared loss and any linear learner shared by all supervisors, we show that a supervisor's value is determined by its errors after they pass through the student's learning operator. Consequently, the inner products of the supervisors' raw errors can be compatible with every feasible value of the student's risk, and weighting supervisors by them can be arbitrarily worse than the best weighting in relative excess risk. This student-relative value is not identifiable from unlabeled data, but what is missing is small: one finite-dimensional projection of the target decides whether training on a weak aggregate helps, another decides how to weight the supervisors. Known teacher training rules, or a label-model condition stated in student-relative form, shrink it further. Clean labels close the remaining gap at a cost set by the geometry of the unresolved directions rather than by the dimension of the student's representation, with matching worst-case lower bounds. In Gaussian designs we also quantify when exact teacher structure beats ordinary stacking and when weak supervisors, combined with clean labels, beat every procedure that uses the clean labels alone. The guarantees extend to fitted ridge students and finite unlabeled data.

items.title: Show HN: Airlock – Policy-as-code for fleets of AI coding agents
items.summary: My name is Matt and I am building Airlock. Airlock is going to be an open standard on managing autonomous fleets of engineering agents. I am seeking constructive feedback on the direction of this project and also asking what are your major pain points with managing AI use at larger businesses. Right now I am running my own company using this framework with a total of 23 workflows across four large scale projects. Airlock is still really early, only 3-4 weeks old. Airlock's configuration standard is aimed to be open source and I will also open source the backplane once I gain a bit more confidence in what I have built here and it is a bit more ready for public scrutiny. Today the schema itself and the reusable GitHub actions are publicly available. I will selfishly figure out how to monetize this at some point but my desired customer is going to be larger enterprises. Airlock kind of does a lot of things but if I had to sum it up in several bullet points it would be: 1) Allows for the configuration of agent behaviors and life cycles under version control. Each agent run proves who it is with GitHub’s OIDC token, and Airlock trades that for a GitHub token that lasts one hour and can only touch the repos and permissions listed in that agent’s role file. 2) Allows for configuring levels of autonomy starting with a repository's base autonomy level with stricter overrides down to individual files within a code base. (e.g. you trust agents for most of the repo but perhaps you want extra gating around the 'billing' or 'auth' modules). 3) Supports a standard autonomy scale. At level 4 agents are leading a project's direction while at level 1 they are dependent on humans to lead the direction of a project. 4) Provides an out-of-the-box OTEL collector that stores a subset of agent actions you would care about in the event of an audit. I’m exploring storing agent prompts and user prompts so that only the customer can decrypt them, and haven’t decided how. 5) Comes with a shadow mode that allows you to run Airlock and observe how it would behave in your org without turning it on. To try it you just need to install the GitHub App, create a policy repository and run on GitHub hosted runners. I personally use self-hosted runners on EC2 spot instances. Visit https://airlock.lunareng.com/docs/quickstart to get started. I have been really passionate lately about exploring how businesses of the [near] future will effectively manage autonomous development using agents at scale. I want to help answer the question of how can the business better manage AI spend, prioritization of token usage, auditability of agent actions and compliance with various governance, risk and compliance frameworks. I am coming from the perspective of being an engineer for 15+ years but I have somehow managed to also develop a good understanding of how larger businesses operate. My vision of the future looks like a world where engineers don't use agent harnesses directly from their computer [for coding]. Instead engineering teams are managing a larger backlog of work that is automatically picked up by these agents. Engineering will instead be less about writing code and more about effectively deploying technology to solve business problems. Thanks for taking a look and I look forward to meeting you in the comments. items.title: Ask HN: How do you manage your AI agents' context across clients and projects?
items.summary: Hi Guys, like many of you I work with AI agents every day and across several clients. The major time cost for me is to re-explaining context and past decisions, client rules, that we already do. To finish every tools as its own memory. So I’m curious how you actually handle this: 1. When you start a new session, how do you give context to the agent (context came from chat, mail, ticket ...) ? 2. Do you use more than one agent type (claude, codex ...) ? And if yes, how do you carry context between agents ? 3. If you work for several clients, how do you keep their context separate ? 4. The last time something went wrong ( an agent used a rejected approach, forgot a decision ...), what happened, and how much time did it cost to you ? 5. Did you paid or built a tool that helped you with these problems ? Do you still use it ? I’m exploring whether to build something, so I’m trying to learn how other people really work. items.title: Show HN: JavaScript web apps with WASM layout and GPU rendering in 280 KB
items.summary: Over the past year, I have been working to find a better way to write cross-platform apps. The problems I am trying to solve: - Native frameworks only work on a subset of platforms, so a different implementation of the UI needs to be written per target. - They are updated at the same pace as the platform itself, which forces the developer to split the user base to be able to use new features, or wait a long time for bugs to get fixed. - They also force developers to use specific high-level languages, so they are not a good fit for apps with high performance requirements, like creative apps or games. - Cross-platform frameworks that rely on bundling a browser engine solve the problem of code reuse, but they inherit the limitations of HTML/CSS. - Those that take control over layout and rendering are not efficient and lightweight enough to be used on the web, and require the use of compiled languages. Ideally, we would be able to bundle the UI framework directly with the application. This would allow developers to use new features and fix issues in the UI framework immediately. It would also allow ideas for improvements to compete in a natural way, rather than being decided by a committee. Uniform is my idea for how we can solve these problems. This is the structure: - A layout and rendering engine written in C, compiled to WASM on the web and native code on all other platforms - A JavaScript API where each function call gets forwarded directly into the core, for best performance and efficiency - A native runtime ( Uniform supports very fast iteration cycles via hot-reload on all platforms. Even on iOS, the JS source code of an app can be changed while the app is running. Changes are visible on the next display refresh. No connection to a computer or the internet is required. Apps can be written from scratch on a phone, with native performance. The readme in the linked repository includes many examples and a detailed explanation of the core ideas. It is handwritten without any use of AI. And here is a live demo: https://raffk.com/hn-demo/ It should work in any browser that supports WebGPU. (To get 120 Hz support in Safari, the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” feature flag needs to be disabled.) I'm planning to develop this further for downstream use cases, maybe try to improve FPS for video and performance on different hardware.
